title: Axial and Appendicular Skeleton
subject: Musculoskeletal System (MUSC)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers the bones of the spine, skull, and limbs and explains how their shapes follow from the work each region does. It relates regional vertebral features to movement and load, the normal spinal curves to their abnormal forms and to breathing, the skull openings to the nerves and vessels that pass through them, and the limb bones to the nerves and arteries that lie against them. Board questions usually describe a fracture, a curve, or a cranial nerve deficit and ask which structure is involved or what function is lost. If you know where each nerve touches bone and why each region is shaped as it is, most of these questions can be reasoned out rather than memorized.

connections.how: The bony features in this chapter are the attachment sites and articular surfaces that set each joint's range and each muscle's action.
Fracture sites, osteoporotic vertebral collapse, and avascular necrosis follow directly from bone shape and blood supply.

sections.title: Regional features of the vertebrae and what each region does

blocks.text: A typical vertebra has a body in front for weight bearing and a vertebral arch behind (pedicles and laminae) enclosing the vertebral foramen, with transverse and spinous processes as muscle levers and paired articular processes forming the facet (zygapophyseal) joints. Body size, which rises with load, and facet orientation best explain what each region can do.

Cervical vertebrae carry only the head, so their bodies are small, and their oblique facets allow the widest range of flexion, extension, lateral flexion, and rotation. Each transverse process has a transverse foramen. The vertebral artery, the first branch of the subclavian artery, usually enters at C6 and rises through the foramina of C6 to C1 before entering the skull through the foramen magnum; C7's foramen usually carries only small veins. The bony canal shields the artery as the neck moves, but cervical fractures can tear or dissect it, causing brainstem or cerebellar stroke. C3 to C6 have short, usually bifid spines that anchor the ligamentum nuchae, and C7 (vertebra prominens) has the long single spine felt at the base of the neck.

The atlas (C1) is a ring of anterior and posterior arches and two lateral masses with no body and no spinous process; its superior facets cradle the occipital condyles, and the atlanto-occipital joints allow nodding. During development the body that would have belonged to C1 joins C2 as the dens, a peg that projects into the ring of the atlas. The atlas pivots around the dens at the atlantoaxial joints, which supply about half of cervical rotation. The transverse ligament of the atlas holds the dens against the anterior arch; if rheumatoid arthritis erodes it, ligament laxity in Down syndrome weakens it, or the dens fractures, C1 can slip forward on C2 and the dens can compress the upper cord.

Thoracic vertebrae carry the ribs. A typical rib head articulates with two adjacent bodies, so typical thoracic bodies have upper and lower costal facets (demifacets), and the transverse processes of T1 to T10 have facets for the rib tubercles. Near-coronal facets allow rotation, but the rib cage splints the region and the long, overlapping spines limit extension. Lumbar vertebrae carry the whole upper body, so they have the largest, kidney-shaped bodies and no transverse foramina or costal facets. Their curved, near-sagittal facets interlock, allowing flexion and extension but nearly blocking rotation. Because the cord ends at about L1 to L2 in adults, the lumbar canal holds the cauda equina, and the heavily loaded L4 to L5 and L5 to S1 discs are the commonest levels of herniation.

blocks.predict: A woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis develops neck pain, brisk reflexes, and weakness in all four limbs. Which structure has failed?
blocks.explain: Synovitis has eroded the transverse ligament of the atlas, so C1 slides forward on C2 and the dens compresses the upper cervical cord, giving upper motor neuron signs in all four limbs.

sections.title: Normal spinal curves, scoliosis, and hyperkyphosis

blocks.text: Seen from the side, the adult column has four curves: cervical lordosis, thoracic kyphosis, lumbar lordosis, and sacral kyphosis. The kyphoses are primary curves, the remnants of the flexed C-shape of the fetus, and come mainly from the shape of the vertebral bodies. The lordoses are secondary curves that come mainly from wedge-shaped discs; they begin before birth and become obvious when the infant holds up its head (cervical) and when the child sits, stands, and walks (lumbar). The alternating curves absorb axial shock like a spring, and the lordoses keep the center of gravity over the hips so standing needs little muscle work.

Excessive thoracic kyphosis (hyperkyphosis) in older adults most often follows osteoporotic compression fractures. Vertebral bodies are mostly trabecular bone, which osteoporosis thins early, and under flexion load the front of the body collapses into a wedge, so height falls and the back rounds. In adolescents, wedging of several adjacent vertebrae gives a rigid kyphosis (Scheuermann disease), and spinal tuberculosis destroys vertebral bodies to give a sharp angular gibbus. Excessive lumbar lordosis follows a forward shift of the center of gravity, as in late pregnancy.

Scoliosis is a lateral curve of at least 10 degrees (Cobb angle) combined with vertebral rotation, so it is a three-dimensional deformity, not simple side bending. The bodies rotate toward the convex side and the spinous processes toward the concavity, and the attached ribs are pushed backward on the convex side, producing a rib hump when the patient bends forward. A structural curve has fixed rotation and persists on bending; a functional curve from a short leg or muscle spasm has no fixed rotation and corrects when the cause is removed. About 80% of structural cases are idiopathic, mostly in adolescents, and progressive curves are far more common in girls. Other causes are hemivertebrae, neuromuscular disease (cerebral palsy, Duchenne muscular dystrophy), and Marfan syndrome.

Severe thoracic scoliosis restricts the lungs from outside. The rotated ribs crowd together on the concave side, the chest wall stiffens (low compliance), and the inspiratory muscles work at a mechanical disadvantage. The lungs and airways themselves are normal, so total lung capacity, vital capacity, and FVC fall while FEV1 falls in proportion, leaving FEV1/FVC normal or high. Function is usually clearly impaired once a thoracic curve passes about 70 degrees. Patients take small, rapid breaths, which raises the dead space fraction; alveolar hypoventilation, worst in sleep, causes hypercapnia and hypoxemia, and chronic hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction leads to pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale. Curves beginning before about age 5 also limit alveolar growth.

blocks.predict: A 19-year-old with a 95 degree thoracic scoliosis has spirometry. Predict FVC, FEV1, and FEV1/FVC, and say how the pattern differs from COPD.
blocks.explain: FVC and FEV1 both fall, FEV1/FVC is normal or high, and TLC is low (extrapulmonary restriction). COPD lowers FEV1 more than FVC, so the ratio falls and TLC is normal or high.

sections.title: Skull foramina, their contents, and the pterion

blocks.text: The cranial base steps down in three fossae. Openings in the sphenoid lead to the orbit, face, and jaw; posterior fossa openings carry the lower cranial nerves, the great veins, and the brainstem.

All three nerves that move the eye and the ophthalmic nerve, which carries sensation from the eyeball and forehead, enter the orbit through the superior orbital fissure, between the greater and lesser wings of the sphenoid: the oculomotor (III), trochlear (IV), ophthalmic (V1), and abducens (VI) nerves, with the superior ophthalmic vein draining back to the cavernous sinus. A lesion here causes ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, loss of pupillary constriction, and forehead and corneal numbness, but spares vision because the optic nerve runs separately through the optic canal. The maxillary nerve (V2) runs forward through the foramen rotundum to the pterygopalatine fossa, and the mandibular nerve (V3), the only trigeminal division with motor fibers, drops through the foramen ovale to the infratemporal fossa. Just behind the ovale, the foramen spinosum admits the middle meningeal artery.

In the posterior fossa, the facial (VII) and vestibulocochlear (VIII) nerves enter the internal acoustic meatus. VII then runs through the facial canal and exits at the stylomastoid foramen, so a vestibular schwannoma in the meatus causes one-sided hearing loss and tinnitus before facial weakness. The jugular foramen transmits IX, X, and XI with the internal jugular vein, and the foramen magnum transmits the medulla, the vertebral arteries, and the spinal roots of XI, so tonsils herniating through it compress the medullary respiratory centers.

blocks.text: The pterion is the H-shaped junction where the frontal, parietal, and squamous temporal bones meet the greater wing of the sphenoid, a short distance above the zygomatic arch. The bone is thin, and on its inner surface, in a groove or sometimes a bony canal, runs the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery, a branch of the maxillary artery that entered through the foramen spinosum. A blow to the temple fractures this thin plate, and the fracture edge tears the artery. Arterial blood strips the periosteal dura from bone, but that layer is fused firmly at the sutures, so the collection is biconvex (lens-shaped) and does not cross suture lines, unlike the crescent of a venous subdural hematoma.

blocks.title: Reasoning from a temple injury
blocks.text: A 17-year-old struck on the left temple by a baseball is briefly unconscious, then lucid. Three hours later he is drowsy, with a dilated, unreactive left pupil and right-sided weakness. The temple overlies the pterion, so the likely injury is a fracture tearing the middle meningeal artery. The brief unconsciousness is concussion; the hematoma then needs time to strip dura from bone and reach a damaging size, hence the lucid interval. The growing mass pushes the left uncus over the tentorium, compressing the left oculomotor nerve (superficial parasympathetic fibers first) and the left cerebral peduncle, whose corticospinal fibers serve the right side.

sections.title: Bones of the upper limb and the nerves at risk in humeral fractures

blocks.text: The upper limb's only bony link to the trunk is the clavicle at the sternoclavicular joint. The S-shaped clavicle is a strut that holds the limb away from the trunk and passes force to the axial skeleton; it often fractures, after which the sternocleidomastoid lifts the medial fragment and the limb's weight drops the shoulder. The scapula glides on the chest wall; its acromion joins the clavicle, and its shallow glenoid gives the shoulder great range but little bony stability. The humerus has a head, anatomical neck, greater and lesser tubercles for rotator cuff tendons, and the narrower surgical neck below them; the shaft bears the deltoid tuberosity and radial groove, and the distal end the capitulum (for the radius), trochlea (for the ulna), and two epicondyles.

In the forearm the radius lies laterally (thumb side) and the ulna medially. The ulna is large at the elbow, where the olecranon and trochlear notch grip the trochlea of the humerus as a hinge, and small at the wrist. The radius is small at the elbow, where its head spins in the annular ligament during pronation and supination, and large at the wrist, where it carries the scaphoid and lunate. The carpals form two rows (proximal: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform; distal: trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate) arched into the carpal tunnel. The scaphoid bridges both rows and is the carpal most often fractured; its vessels enter mainly distally, so a waist fracture can leave the proximal pole without blood, causing nonunion and avascular necrosis. The lunate, the carpal most often dislocated, can compress the median nerve in the tunnel.

Three nerves lie directly on the humerus, so the fracture site predicts the nerve. The axillary nerve winds around the surgical neck, which often breaks when an older adult with osteoporosis falls; injury weakens the deltoid and teres minor (abduction beyond the first 15 degrees) and numbs skin over the lower deltoid. The radial nerve spirals along the radial groove on the back of the shaft, so a midshaft fracture paralyzes the wrist and finger extensors (wrist drop) and numbs the back of the hand near the first web space; triceps is usually spared because most of its branches leave the nerve above the groove. The ulnar nerve runs behind the medial epicondyle, so a fracture there weakens most intrinsic hand muscles, giving weak finger abduction and adduction, clawing of the ring and little fingers, and numbness of the medial one and a half digits. The clawing is often milder than with a wrist lesion because an elbow lesion also weakens the medial flexor digitorum profundus, which would otherwise flex the distal joints.

blocks.title: Predicting the nerve from the fracture
blocks.text: A 45-year-old falls from a ladder and has a midshaft fracture of the humerus. He cannot extend his wrist or fingers but can extend his elbow, and the back of the hand near the thumb is numb. The radial nerve lies in the radial groove on the back of the midshaft, so it is the nerve at risk. Wrist and finger extensors are supplied below the groove and are lost; triceps branches mostly leave the nerve higher, so elbow extension survives.

sections.title: Bones of the lower limb, the foot arches, and the common fibular nerve

blocks.text: Each hip bone forms from the ilium, ischium, and pubis, which meet in the acetabulum and are joined by a Y-shaped (triradiate) cartilage until they fuse in adolescence. With the sacrum and pubic symphysis, the hip bones form a ring that carries weight from the spine to the femurs in standing and to the ischial tuberosities in sitting. The deep acetabulum and its labrum hold most of the femoral head, trading range for stability.

The femur is the longest and strongest bone. Its neck meets the shaft at about 125 degrees in adults, giving hip muscles leverage, and the shaft angles medially so the knees sit under the body. Most blood reaches the adult femoral head through retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery running up the neck inside the capsule, so a displaced neck fracture risks avascular necrosis of the head. The tibia carries body weight from the femur to the talus and, because its anteromedial surface lies under the skin, often has open fractures; the slender fibula bears little weight, anchors muscles, and forms the lateral malleolus.

The common fibular (peroneal) nerve, a terminal branch of the sciatic nerve, winds around the fibular neck under only skin and fascia. A fibular neck fracture, a tight cast, or habitual leg crossing can injure it. Its deep branch supplies the ankle dorsiflexors and toe extensors and the skin of the first web space, and its superficial branch supplies the evertors (fibularis longus and brevis) and most skin of the dorsum of the foot. Injury therefore causes foot drop with a high-stepping gait, loss of eversion, and numbness over the dorsum of the foot, while plantar flexion and inversion by tibialis posterior, both supplied by the tibial nerve, remain.

The foot bones form arches that spread weight between heel and metatarsal heads and let the foot act as a shock absorber in stance and a rigid lever at push-off. The medial longitudinal arch is the highest, with the head of the talus as its keystone. It is held passively by the plantar calcaneonavicular (spring) ligament, which cradles the talar head, and by the plantar aponeurosis, which ties heel to toes like a bowstring, and actively by the tibialis posterior tendon. When the toes dorsiflex at push-off, the aponeurosis winds around the metatarsal heads, shortening the foot and raising the arch.

Pes planus (flat foot) is a low or collapsed medial longitudinal arch. Infants look flat-footed because of a plantar fat pad, and a flexible flat foot whose arch reappears on tiptoe is usually painless. Acquired adult flat foot most often follows tibialis posterior tendon failure (below); a rigid flat foot, as with fused tarsals (tarsal coalition), has a structural cause.

blocks.predict: After a tight below-knee cast, a patient catches his toes when walking. Which movements are weak, which are preserved, and where is skin numb?
blocks.explain: Pressure at the fibular neck injures the common fibular nerve. Dorsiflexion and toe extension (deep branch) and eversion (superficial branch) are weak; plantar flexion and inversion by tibialis posterior (tibial nerve) remain. The dorsum of the foot is numb.

integration.text: Embryology and histology explain much of the anatomy. The dens is the displaced body of C1, primary and secondary curves record fetal flexion and later upright posture, and hemivertebrae from defective somite segmentation (MS-1) cause congenital scoliosis. Vertebral bodies, the femoral neck, and the distal radius are rich in trabecular bone, which osteoporosis thins first (MS-13-C), so they are where fragility fractures cluster. Blood supply that enters bone from one end, as in the scaphoid and femoral head, explains avascular necrosis after fracture, and infection or inflammation that erodes ligaments, such as rheumatoid destruction of the transverse ligament of the atlas (MS-11), turns a stable joint into a threat to the spinal cord.

Physiology and pathology follow from position. A nerve or vessel that lies on bone or passes through a foramen is injured when that bone breaks or the opening narrows, so a grouped deficit points to one site: III, IV, V1, and VI to the superior orbital fissure; IX, X, and XI to the jugular foramen; extensors with spared triceps to the radial groove. Severe scoliosis links the skeleton to respiratory and cardiac physiology through restriction, hypoventilation, and hypoxic pulmonary hypertension. Anatomical variation limits these rules: the vertebral artery sometimes enters above C6, and the middle meningeal artery may run in a bony canal, so the expected structure is the most likely one, not a certainty.

summary: Cervical vertebrae have transverse foramina for the vertebral artery (usually C6 to C1) and bifid spines; the atlas has no body, and the dens of the axis is the pivot for head rotation.
Thoracic costal facets carry the ribs, and the rib cage limits thoracic motion; large lumbar bodies bear weight and sagittal lumbar facets permit flexion and extension but block rotation.
Thoracic and sacral kyphoses are primary curves; cervical and lumbar lordoses are secondary curves formed with head control and walking.
Scoliosis is lateral curvature with vertebral rotation; hyperkyphosis is an exaggerated sagittal curve, often from osteoporotic wedge fractures.
Severe thoracic scoliosis stiffens the chest wall, lowering TLC and vital capacity with normal FEV1/FVC, and can progress to hypoventilation and cor pulmonale.

Superior orbital fissure: III, IV, V1, VI. Rotundum: V2. Ovale: V3. Spinosum: middle meningeal artery. Internal acoustic meatus: VII and VIII. Jugular foramen: IX, X, XI and internal jugular vein. Foramen magnum: medulla and vertebral arteries.
A fracture of the thin pterion tears the middle meningeal artery, producing a biconvex epidural hematoma that does not cross sutures and can cause uncal herniation.
Humeral surgical neck fractures injure the axillary nerve, midshaft fractures the radial nerve (wrist drop), and medial epicondyle fractures the ulnar nerve.
Scaphoid waist and femoral neck fractures risk avascular necrosis because blood reaches the vulnerable fragment from one direction only.
Fibular neck fractures injure the common fibular nerve (foot drop, lost eversion); collapse of the medial longitudinal arch, often from tibialis posterior failure, causes pes planus.

verify: Thresholds for scoliosis vary: 10 degrees Cobb angle defines scoliosis; the angle above which lung function is clearly impaired is quoted from about 60 to 80 degrees; this chapter uses about 70 degrees.
The proportion of structural scoliosis that is idiopathic (about 80%) and the female predominance of progressive curves vary among sources.
The share of cervical rotation at the atlantoaxial joints is quoted as about half (some sources give 50% to 60%).
The vertebral artery enters the transverse foramen of C6 in most people (often quoted as about 90%) but may enter at C5, C4, or C7.
The age of fusion of the triradiate cartilage is given variously from about 14 to 17 years; this chapter says adolescence.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects the eponym Scheuermann disease or only the descriptive term (adolescent structural kyphosis from vertebral wedging).
